references.supports: The printing question. The Diarium is the first true book from the Uraniborg press: 4to, 30 leaves, signed Aa1-Dd4 A4-C4 D3 — a signing pattern proving the last 14 leaves (the calendar) were printed first, hence probably in late 1585; 2,000 copies were planned, on paper Tycho had to beg from Henrik Rantzau (letter of 8 Jan. 1585); the book opens with the author's dedication to the not-quite-nine-year-old Crown Prince Christian dated 1 January 1586, followed by an astrological preface, then the comet sections; colophon 'IMPRESSVM VRANIBVRGI IN INSVLA CELEBRIS PORTHMI DANICI HVAENA'; no year on the title-page; three copies at the Royal Library, Copenhagen, one containing a leaf with Tycho's autograph dedication to Albert Meier. Nielsen does not mention the draft — it was not printed.

references.source: Nielsen 1931 and Nielsen 1921
references.locus: s.a. 1586, 'Diarium astrologicum et methorologicum anni 1586'
references.supports: Negative evidence for the printing status of the draft: Nielsen's complete enumeration of the Uraniborg press's output contains the Diarium (under Morsing) but no separate printing of any prefatory draft by Tycho. Corroborates the 2,000-copy print run, the imported paper, the SVSPICIENDO DESPICIO emblem, and the dedication to Prince Christian.

references.source: John Robert Christianson, On Tycho's Island: Tycho Brahe and His Assistants, 1570–1601 (Cambridge, 2000) — Part Two, Biographical Directory, s.v. 'MORSING, ELIAS OLSEN'
references.supports: Identification of the nominal author: Elias Olsen Morsing (Helias, Elias Olai Cymber, Morsianus), b. c. 1550 on the island of Mors, leading assistant to Tycho on Hven 1583-90, sent to Frombork in 1584 to redetermine the latitude of Copernicus's observatory and given Copernicus's triquetrum, died on Hven 11 March 1590. Also: 'In 1585, Morsing was assigned by Tycho Brahe to prepare an astrological calendar for 1586, which Tycho wanted to print in some two thousand copies on his new press... The printing was dated 1 January 1586, and the work came out under the name of Morsing. It was the first bound product of the Uraniborg press' — and the comet appendix was 'written in part by Tycho'. Christianson elsewhere calls it plainly 'the 1586 almanac by Tycho and Morsing' (p. 300).

references.source: Dreyer's Prolegomena to TBOO X, with TBOO IV
references.locus: entry on the 1586 Diarium apparatus
references.supports: Corroboration of the manuscript identification: in Cod. Vindob. lat. 10689(6) the preface addressing Prince Christian is 'aliqua ex parte Tychonis manu adumbratam' (partly drafted in Tycho's hand), and two diary pages ('De Aestate', 'De Autumno') carry corrections manu Tychonis.

open_questions: Exactly which piece of the printed front matter the sketch underlies is not settled. Nielsen distinguishes two things in the printed book — a DEDICATION by the author to Prince Christian dated 1 January 1586, and then 'en astrologisk Fortale' — whereas Dreyer speaks of a single 'praefatio libelli' addressing the prince. The draft's content (an astrological encomium building to an exhortation of the prince) fits the Fortale, but Dreyer nowhere collates the two and the point is left open here rather than resolved by inference.

How much of Morsing's finished preface actually follows Tycho's sketch is unknown and cannot be checked in TBOO: Dreyer says the execution was mostly left to Morsing ('Eliae arbitrio plerumque permissum'), and TBOO prints only the draft (IX 147-150) and the comet section (IV 397-414), never the printed preface itself. A collation would require the Uraniborg imprint (KB Copenhagen holds three copies).

The extent of the autograph is stated only loosely. TBOO IV p. 513 says the preface was found 'aliqua ex parte' sketched in Tycho's hand; neither TBOO IV nor TBOO IX says whether the whole of the four printed pages is autograph or only part, nor identifies the hand of any non-autograph portion.

The draft contains an internal dating hint that is not followed up by Dreyer: 'Quod felici et firmo sidere ante annum electus sit' — the prince is said to have been elected about a year before writing. Which act of election or homage is meant (and therefore what precise year the sketch belongs to) is not established by any authority consulted here, and no guess is recorded.

The DSL Tekstnet edition (Zeeberg / Gredal Jensen), which carries 21 editorial notes on this text, was not consulted — the edition was not consulted directly — so it is unknown whether its editors depart from Dreyer on the codex, the date, or the relation of draft to printed preface.
editorial_notes: Addressee not named in the draft itself; identified as Crown Prince Christian via the printed 1586 Diarium's dedication (Nielsen) and internal evidence (addressee 'elected a year before' = the 1584 hyldning; oration to proceed to his grandfather and father)

works.title: Inscriptiones Croneburgensis
works.title_full: Inscriptiones Croneburgenses
works.gloss: Latin verse inscriptions composed for Kronborg castle, praising its builder King Frederick II and Queen Sophie and adding a distich on fleeting time for the clock tablet.

date.basis: tekstnet's own subtitle dates the work '(c. 1586)'; the edition's year 1586
date.note: No source dates either piece. Dreyer prints them undated and unannotated as to date (TBOO IX pp. 190–191; the Annotationes editorum at p. 323 discuss only where the first one stood). The 1586 comes from the edition, whose metadata heads the text 'Inscriptiones Croneburgensis / Indskrifter fra Kronborg (c. 1586)'; the grounds for that year are not stated in its metadata. The range given here is the interval the text itself supports. Floor: the poem speaks of a completed and fortified castle ('Structurae tanta mole peregit opus, / Munivitque arcem, velut adspicis') — Frederik II's modernisation of the fortifications round the medieval Krogen ran through the 1570s (the works were renamed Kronborg in 1577) and the rebuilding of the castle proper was carried to 1585 (Vellev, Renaessanceforum 12 [2017], pp. 108–109). Ceiling: the poem prays for the living king's long life and for his descendants' long possession of the house, so it is earlier than Frederik II's death on 4 April 1588, which Tycho marked in separate epigrams (TBOO IX p. 192; Dreyer's note, p. 323). Anything narrower than c. 1585–1588 would be invention.

works.summary: Two Latin inscriptions from Kronborg castle at Elsinore, printed together by Dreyer under the rubric INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES. The first is twenty-four lines (twelve elegiac distichs) spoken from the building to the beholder ('velut adspicis'): the renowned FRIDERICUS, 'second both in name and in fortune', founded this lofty castle — a king pious, just, mild, strong in arms yet one who unwillingly preferred arms to the toga — whose queen SOPHIA, born of the house of Mecklenburg, bore him children full of grace; in peaceful years he finished the great mass of the structure and fortified the castle, yet not so as to lodge his hope of protection in it, nor to boast, as the builder of Babylon exulted, that human hands made these strongholds — that arrogance paid its penalty when the seventh year saw the man mad and like the beasts (Nebuchadnezzar, Daniel 4) — for the Danish king makes no display, trusting to be safe under God's protection alone, well knowing that without the favour of the Deity no bulwarks avail, not though made of steel and hard adamant; so may the Creator of stars, earth and sea, in whom alone King Frederik places his hope, grant that he, his offspring and his late descendants may long inhabit these houses in firm and flourishing peace. The second is a single distich headed IN TABULA HOROLOGII, for the face of a clock: 'Transvolat hora levis neque scit fugitiva reverti, / Nostra simul properans vita caduca fugit' — the light hour flies past and, a fugitive, does not know how to return; our frail life, hurrying, flees along with it. The first was a placed, carved inscription: Dreyer records that in his own day a tablet was still shown on the outer face of Kronborg's north-facing bastion, on which the poem had been cut, but that the lettering had by then worn away.
works.occasion: The subject is the building of Kronborg — Frederik II's transformation of the medieval Krogen into a fortified renaissance residence, the fortification works of the 1570s and the castle carried to completion by 1585 — and the poem's whole argument is a courtier's theological compliment: the king builds and fortifies, but places his trust in God, not in his walls. That is the *matter*. The *occasion* in the strict sense — who asked Tycho for the verses, when, for what ceremony or dedication, and by whose warrant they were cut into the bastion tablet — is not recoverable from any source consulted here. Dreyer prints the pieces with no occasion, no date and no comment beyond their (lost) physical location; nothing in TBOO XIV's document series, in Nielsen, in Friis 1871, or in the modern literature consulted discusses them. One piece of contemporary context should be recorded and then explicitly not over-read: on 28 September 1585 Frederik II wrote to Gert Rantzau, lensmand of Kronborg, ordering the castle painter to copy for Tycho the portraits of the kings from the great Kronborg tapestries and to have the Danish and German rhymes belonging to them transcribed for him (Friis 1871, p. 151). That shows Tycho in working traffic with Kronborg's decorative and epigraphic programme in precisely the years in question — but no source connects that traffic to these verses, and the inference must not be made. The occasion is unknown.
works.addressee_note: None in the epistolary sense: this is monumental verse, addressed grammatically to the passer-by who looks at the fortified castle ('velut adspicis'), and, in its closing prayer, to God ('det astrorum terraeque marisque Creator'). Its honorands are King Frederik II of Denmark (1534–1588, r. 1559-88), Tycho's patron — the donor of Hven and of Uraniborg's building costs — who is named in the first line and again in line 22, and, jointly with him, his queen, Sophie of Mecklenburg (1557–1631), named in line 6 as 'Mechelburgiaca nata SOPHIA domo'.
works.transmission: No manuscript witness is known and Dreyer names none — unlike the neighbouring Carmina in the same volume, for which he cites the Vienna codex (Vindobonensis lat. 10686) or the Langebek excerpts, these two pieces come to Dreyer from a printed antiquarian source only. His headnote at TBOO IX p. 190 reads '[Ex Erici Pontoppidani Marmoribus Danicis I p. 136 (Hauniae 1739)]': the text descends from the carved tablet at Kronborg through Pontoppidan's collection of Danish inscriptions, printed in Copenhagen in 1739, and from Pontoppidan to Dreyer, who prints the two inscriptions at TBOO IX pp. 190–191 among the Carmina. Dreyer makes exactly one editorial intervention, recorded in the Variae scripturae at TBOO IX p. 314: 'AD INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES. p. 191 v. 2 Structurae e Structura correximus' — i.e. he corrects the source's 'Structura' to 'Structurae' in the line 'Structurae tanta mole peregit opus'. In the Annotationes editorum (TBOO IX p. 323) he adds the only note that exists on the pieces: 'INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES (p. 190 sq.) non jam exstant, sed monstratur etiamnum tabula in exteriore parte propugnaculi adversus septentriones spectantis, cui prior inscriptio insculpta fuit; nunc vero evanuit' — the Kronborg inscriptions no longer exist, but the tablet on the outer face of the north-facing bastion, into which the first of them had been cut, was still shown in his day, its lettering by then effaced. The editors themselves index the group as inscriptions: TBOO XV, Index hominum et rerum, p. 19, 'Croneburgenses inscriptiones IX 190-191'; and s.v. Fridericus II (pp. 22–23), 'Croneburgum condidit IX 190'. That is the entire chain of transmission as the sources give it: stone (lost/effaced) -> Pontoppidan 1739 -> Dreyer 1927.

printed.note: There is no evidence that these verses were ever set in type in Tycho's lifetime. They carry no Nielsen number: they are absent both from Nielsen's enumerated Brahe corpus (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, nos. 424-433 with 975-976) and from his list of the lost/disputed Hveen prints (Carmen ad Falk Gjoee; Carmen ad Erik Lange; the Hans Frandsen elegy; the 1591 Craig Apologia). Their lifetime 'publication' was the stone itself — the tablet cut on the outer face of Kronborg's north bastion (Dreyer, TBOO IX p. 323). The earliest printing traced here is posthumous and late: Erik Pontoppidan, Marmora Danica, tomus I (Hauniae, 1739), p. 136, which is the copy-text named in Dreyer's own headnote, '[Ex Erici Pontoppidani Marmoribus Danicis I p. 136 (Hauniae 1739)]' — 138 years after Tycho's death. TBOO IX (1927) is therefore NOT the first printing. Two negatives are worth recording: the poem is not in Resen's Inscriptiones Hafnienses (1668) — a page-by-page search of Resen finds no 'Inclytus hanc celsam' and no trace of the text, which is consistent with Resen's Copenhagen/Hven scope — and Dreyer cites no other witness. The printer of Pontoppidan's volume is not named in the sources consulted here. See open_questions for the one live possibility of a lifetime printing (Nathan Chytraeus, Herborn 1594).

works.modern_edition: Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab, tekstnet.dk: 'Tycho Brahe: Inscriptiones Croneburgensis / Indskrifter fra Kronborg', ed. Peter Zeeberg and Finn Gredal Jensen, https://tekstnet.dk/books/brahe-t_inscriptiones-croneburgenses/001/ (dated c. 1586). The DSL text follows TBOO IX pp. 190–191, anchors its page-breaks to them, and carries a single text-critical note recording Dreyer's emendation against the source reading ('Structurae] TBOO, Structura A'). No other modern edition, translation or commentary on these two pieces has been found.

open_questions: The date is unsupported. The edition gives c. 1586; no authority consulted here states a year, and Dreyer prints both pieces undated. The c. 1585–1588 range recorded above is inferred from the building history and from Frederik II's death, not documented. If the edition has grounds for 1586 (perhaps from Pontoppidan, or from a year on the stone), they are not stated.

On what basis are the verses Tycho's? This is the record's weakest joint. Dreyer prints them among Tycho's Carmina, but his only citation is Pontoppidan's Marmora Danica (1739) — a collection of Danish carved inscriptions compiled 138 years after Tycho's death — and he nowhere states, in the headnote, the Variae scripturae or the Annotationes, what evidence assigns the poem to Tycho. Whether Pontoppidan himself names Tycho as author, and on what authority, has NOT been verified: Marmora Danica has not been seen for this record. Until it is checked, the ascription rests on Dreyer's editorial decision alone, and is a weaker claim than the text or the transmission.

Was there a lifetime printing after all? Tycho supplied Nathan Chytraeus with the Danish inscriptions for his Variorum in Europa itinerum deliciae (Herborn: Christoph Rab, 1594), which acknowledges the debt in the preface and prints a selection of the Hven inscriptions at pp. 593–601 (Vellev 2017). Whether the Kronborg tablet — a royal inscription that Tycho, if he wrote it, would have been well placed to supply — is among Chytraeus's Danica has not been checked; the book has not been seen for this record, and Dreyer does not cite it. If it is there, the printing status of this record changes from posthumous (1739) to printed in Tycho's lifetime (1594). This is the single most valuable next check.

Where was the clock inscription? The rubric IN TABULA HOROLOGII gives the fitting but not the building; Dreyer's note specifies the placement only of the 'prior inscriptio' (the bastion tablet) and says merely that the Kronborg inscriptions 'non jam exstant'. That the clock in question was Kronborg's is the natural reading of the shared rubric and of Pontoppidan's context, but no source says so. Note that Tycho used the same conceit at Uraniborg, where a distich ran round the rim of the cupola clock (TBOO VI p. 369).

Does the bastion tablet still exist? Dreyer reported in 1927 that it was 'still shown' on the outer face of the north-facing bastion with its letters effaced. No modern report — archaeological, conservation, or Kronborg-museum — has been checked; whether the stone survives, and whether raking-light or photogrammetric re-reading could recover any of the lettering (as Vellev and Zeeberg did in 2001 for Tycho's Hven paper-mill votive stone), is unknown.

Title form: TBOO's rubric and the TBOO XV index give the plural 'Inscriptiones Croneburgenses'; the edition heads the piece 'Inscriptiones Croneburgensis'. The plural is Dreyer's and is adopted here; nothing of substance hangs on it, but the variant should be kept searchable.

The 'work' is an editorial grouping, not a Tycho-authored collection: two separate inscriptions, of very different scale and character (a 24-line dynastic-theological poem for a bastion; a two-line memento-fugit for a clock-face), printed under one rubric because Pontoppidan found them together at Kronborg.
editorial_notes: The edition's display title has the form 'Croneburgensis'; the text's own heading reads INSCRIPTIONES CRONEBURGENSES.

works.title_en: Four epigrams on the death of Frederick II
works.gloss: Four Latin epigrams on the death of King Frederick II (4 April 1588), the first two written as chronograms with the date concealed in their capitalised numeral-letters.

date.basis: The epigrams themselves date the death to 4 April of the eighty-eighth year ('quarto aprilis', 'octogesimus octavus annus Christi'); the edition's year 1588.

works.title: Apologetica responsio ad Craigum Scotum de cometis
works.title_full: Apologetica responsio ad Craigum Scotum de cometis (heading in the Copenhagen codex, printed by Dreyer at the head of the text: 'Apologia illustriss. viri domini Tychonis Brahe ad Craigum Scotum de cometis'; fuller heading in the Berlin codex: 'Apologia Dn. Tychonis Brahe ad D. Johannem Craigum, qva ipsius placita disqviruntur & redarguuntur'; Erasmus Bartholin's 1665 citation-form of the printed edition: 'Apologetica responsio ad cujusdam Peripatetici in Scotia dubia, sibi de parallaxi cometarum opposita')
works.title_en: Apologetic reply to the Scot Craig concerning comets
works.gloss: Tycho's reply to the Scottish mathematician John Craig, defending against Craig's objections the argument of his De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis (1588) that comets are celestial bodies above the moon.

date.basis: the edition's year 1589; a reply to Craig's critique of De mundi (printed 1588, Nielsen).
date.note: Composition is fixed within 1589 by the correspondence at both ends. John Craig's three letters of objection are of May, 18 June and 9 July 1589 (TBOO VII, pp. 175–182, 191-193, 193; Dreyer's note ad p. 474,5, TBOO IV, p. 521); Tycho 'immediately composed a copious Apologetica Responsio' ('At Tycho continuo Apologeticam Responsionem copiosam composuit', TBOO IV, p. 517) and sent it to Craig with his letter of 25 October 1589 (TBOO VII, pp. 195–196). Dreyer's own head-title dates the piece '(1589)'. Note that 1589 is the year of WRITING; the (lost) Uraniborg printing is of 1591, and a further Hamburg/Wandsbek printing is reported for 1598 — see 'printed'. Tycho himself says he dictated it to an amanuensis between other business, 'prout in buccam venerunt' (as the words came into his mouth), which explains its unevenness (Tycho to Hagecius, 25 January 1590, quoted TBOO IV, p. 518).

works.summary: A long polemical treatise-in-address (some sixty printed pages in TBOO; Mosley calls it 'a forty-page document'), cast as a continuous reply to a named opponent and answering, point by point, the objections John Craig had raised in three letters against Tycho's De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis (1588). It opens with elaborate courtesy — 'Pergratus mihi fuit tuus ille eruditus labor... Doctissime CRAIGE' — thanking Craig for having examined the book so closely, since truth 'shines out more clearly only when what can be adduced against it has been weighed in a just balance', and then registers Tycho's astonishment that a man so skilled in mathematics should be so enslaved to Aristotle's authority. The substance is a defence of the two claims Craig had attacked: that the comet of 1577 showed no sensible parallax and therefore stood far beyond the Moon in the ether (Craig held that the comet's own proper motion vitiated Tycho's parallax determinations), and that there are no solid celestial orbs — the planets move freely through a fluid heaven, the Earth resting immobile at the centre. It closes by defending the Tychonic hypotheses (Mars at acronychal rising nearer the Earth than the Sun), by referring to the circelli Tycho had explained to Duncan Liddel ('Dunchanus'), and by inviting Craig to weigh the whole 'per otium justa ingenii et judicii trutina'.
works.occasion: Fully recoverable. In 1588 a Scottish soldier-diplomat of James VI, William Stewart of Houston, visited Uraniborg; when he sailed home he carried a presentation copy of Tycho's De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis (1588) inscribed by Tycho to John Craig, physician in Edinburgh, 'Vraniburgi anno 1588 Nouemb. 2.' — the copy still in Edinburgh University Library (Dreyer, TBOO IV, pp. 515–516). Craig thanked Tycho and, in three letters of May-July 1589, raised Aristotelian objections: comets are sublunary phenomena of the air, and Tycho's parallax argument is invalid because it fails to allow for the comet's own motion; the abolition of the solid spheres is also rejected. Tycho answered at once with this Apologia and despatched it with a (deliberately genial) covering letter of 25 October 1589. Dreyer's judgement of the whole affair: 'this gift gave occasion to the contest between Tycho and Craig on the nature of comets; had it not existed, Craig's name would scarcely have been handed down to posterity' (TBOO IV, p. 516). Almost immediately Tycho conceived a further, editorial occasion for the piece: he decided to print it, together with Craig's letters, as an appendix to De mundi liber secundus, and told Hagecius (25 Jan and 23 Feb 1590), Peucer (1590 or 1591) and Craig himself (14 Nov 1591) so (TBOO IV, p. 517).
works.addressee_note: John Craig (Joannes Craigius, d. 1620), Scottish physician and mathematician, at the time of the dispute practising medicine in Edinburgh; later physician to James VI and, after 1603, a member of the London Royal College of Physicians (1604) and incorporated M.D. at Oxford (1605). He had taught mathematics and logic at the University of Frankfurt an der Oder — Duncan Liddel was his pupil there before going to Wrocław to learn mathematics from Paul Wittich — and returned to Scotland in 1584; he never visited Denmark. He was the younger brother of the jurist Thomas Craig, who in 1594 wrote to Tycho to apologise for him. (Dreyer, TBOO IV, pp. 516–517; Mosley, 'Tycho Brahe and John Craig', 2002, p. 75 and n. 22; Familia, s.v. John Craig, where he is one of Westman's four Tycho disputants — Ursus, Wittich, Rothmann, Craig — and the man whose transcription of a Wittich note supplied the key to the Wittich hand.) A secondary addressee is the learned public: the Praefatio Tycho later drafted for the projected printed edition speaks past Craig to the 'optime et benevole Lector' (TBOO IX, p. 156).
works.transmission: The words survive in manuscript, not in the print. Dreyer's source-lemma (TBOO IV, p. 416) states the position exactly: the Apologetica Responsio, 'written in 1589 and printed at Uraniborg in 1591, since not even one printed exemplar appears to survive, we edit from the Copenhagen codex Nov. Coll. Reg. 93b in folio; we have also collated a manuscript fragment appended to the Berlin exemplar of the first book of the Progymnasmata and of De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis.' The Copenhagen manuscript (Kongelige Bibliotek, Ny kgl. Samling 93b fol.) is a fair copy 'written apparently not long after Tycho's time', reasonably accurate; the Berlin witness — the Tycho convolute in the Staatsbibliothek — carries, after the printed De mundi, Craig's three letters entire (nowhere else transmitted) and the FIRST PAGES ONLY of the Apologia (to TBOO IV, p. 421,10). Nielsen argues that this Berlin fragment was copied from the lost printed edition and therefore shows how that edition was made up: Craig's three letters first, then the Apologia (Nielsen 1921, pp. 194–195). Tycho also circulated the piece in manuscript to friends (Hagecius, Peucer, and William Fuller, who read it at Uraniborg). Its first appearance in public print is therefore Dreyer's — 'quae nunc primum in publicum emittitur' (TBOO IV, p. 517) — in Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia, tom. IV (Copenhagen, 1922), pp. 415–476, with the editor's notes at pp. 515–521. Directly attached to it are three further texts, all edited by Dreyer: Craig's three letters and Tycho's covering letter of 25 Oct 1589 (TBOO VII); Craig's counter-attack, the Capnuraniae restinctionis fragmentum (TBOO IV, pp. 477–488), never published by Craig; and the paratexts Tycho drafted for the projected printed edition — the 'Praefatio in Apologiam sequentem', an epilogue on the Capnurania and even a German instruction to the compositor — first printed by Dreyer & Raeder from cod. Vindobonensis lat. 9737f as 'Additamenta ad Apologeticam responsionem ad Craigum Scotum de cometis', TBOO IX (1927), pp. 151–157 (a separate record here: brahe-t_apologetica-responsio-additamenta).
works.channel_basis: the Uraniborg print of 1591, no copy known (Nielsen 1921, pp. 193–195)

printed.printer: Tycho's own press (printer not named; no copy survives to bear a colophon)
printed.nielsen: none — Nielsen assigns no Dansk Bibliografi number, because no copy survives; the printing is established in his 'Tycho Brahes Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen' (1921), pp. 193–195
printed.note: printed IN TYCHO'S LIFETIME, BUT NOT ONE COPY SURVIVES, AND THE PRINTING WAS LONG DENIED. Dreyer states it flatly: after communicating his plan to Hagecius, Peucer and Craig, 'ac re vera a. 1591 Uraniburgi typis descripta est. Sed ne unum quidem exemplum Apologiae typis descriptum ad nostram aetatem pervenisse videtur' (TBOO IV, p. 517). The evidence is Erasmus (Rasmus) Bartholin, De cometis anni MDCLXIV & MDCLXV (Copenhagen, 1665), p. 49, who quotes the work and says he owns the print: '... in Apologetica Responsione ad cujusdam Peripatetici in Scotia dubia, quam impressam habeo Uraniburgi Anno 1591 (neque ut putat eximius Gassendus in Vita Tychonis, Manuscripta tantum reservata est a Longomontano & Frommio)' — an explicit correction of Gassendi, who had said the work survived only in manuscript, kept by Longomontanus and then by Jørgen From. All four passages Bartholin quotes are found in the Copenhagen codex (Dreyer, TBOO IV, p. 517). Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (1668), p. 391, also lists the Apologetica Responsio, with Craig's letter and the Capnurania restinctio, as appended to De mundi liber II — though without saying in so many words that they were printed. The lost print is entered in the older astronomical bibliographies with a title-form matching Bartholin's: Lalande, Bibliographie astronomique (1803), p. 123, and Houzeau & Lancaster, Bibliographie générale de l'astronomie (1887), which calls it 'très rare'. AGAINST this: Gassendi (Vita Tychonis, 1654/55, p. 240 of the Paris ed.), and — before Nielsen's 1921 article — BOTH modern biographers, F. R. Friis (Tyge Brahe, 1871, p. 265) and Dreyer himself (Tycho Brahe, 1890, p. 209 n.; German ed. p. 219), concluded that the Apologia was never printed. Nielsen 1921 overturned that with the Bartholin passage; Dreyer, editing TBOO IV in 1922, cites Nielsen's article and now asserts the 1591 printing as fact. A second, LATER printing is reported but unconfirmed: Houzeau & Lancaster list, after the 1591 Uraniborg edition, a further '[Wandesburgi] 1598', which agrees with Tycho's letter to Bartholomäus Scultetus of 7 January 1600 (from Prague) mentioning 'defensive writings' he had had printed in Hamburg. Nielsen accepts this only tentatively — the 1592 arrival of Craig's Capnuraniae restinctio may have made a revision necessary — and adds 'Forholdet er dog ikke helt klart' (the matter is not entirely clear): Nielsen 1921, p. 195. No copy of any printing is known.

open_questions: Was it in fact printed? The whole printing claim rests on one witness — Rasmus Bartholin's 1665 statement that he owned a printed copy — plus the bibliographies (Lalande 1803, Houzeau & Lancaster 1887) that may simply depend on him, plus Resen 1668 (who does not say in so many words that the pieces were printed). Gassendi (1654/55), Friis (1871) and Dreyer (1890) all denied the printing; Dreyer reversed himself in TBOO IV (1922) after Nielsen's 1921 article. No copy of any printing is known, and no copy has been reported since. The reversal is recorded here rather than smoothed over; that Nielsen's article is what changed Dreyer's mind is a plausible inference (Dreyer cites it in TBOO IV, p. 491 n. 3) but is not stated by Dreyer.

The reported second printing, '[Wandesburgi] 1598' (Houzeau & Lancaster), is unverified. Its only corroboration is Tycho's own reference, in his letter to Scultetus of 7 January 1600, to 'defensive writings' printed at Hamburg — which he says he intends to print AGAIN, since a further refutation of 'a learned Scot' has still to be added. Nielsen accepts it only tentatively and says outright that the matter is not clear. Whether the 1598 item was a reprint of the 1591 Apologia, an enlarged version answering the Capnurania, or something else entirely is unknown.

Who commended Craig to Tycho? Dreyer (TBOO IV, p. 515) says William Stewart of Houston 'seems to have' done so; Mosley (2002, p. 75 n. 21) says Craig's own first letter makes clear that Stewart merely carried the book, and that it was Duncan Liddel who named Craig to Tycho. Mosley's reading rests on the primary letter and should be preferred, but the disagreement stands in the literature.

The relation of the Berlin manuscript fragment to the lost print. Nielsen infers that the Berlin fragment (Craig's three letters + the opening pages of the Apologia, bound after the printed De mundi) was transcribed FROM the printed edition, and uses this to reconstruct that edition's make-up. Dreyer merely uses the fragment as a textual witness and does not endorse the inference. The Berlin shelfmark is not recorded in the sources consulted here.

The exact extent and title of the printed edition are unrecoverable. Dreyer's title 'Apologetica Responsio' is a reconstruction ('illa esse videtur, si Bartholino et Resenio credimus, quam exhibuit editio typis descripta'); the two surviving manuscripts give different headings, and Tycho in his letters sometimes says simply 'Apologia'.

Nothing establishes how far the printed 1591 text differed from the Copenhagen codex Dreyer printed. Bartholin's four quotations are all found in the codex, which is reassuring but not decisive; and the Additamenta (TBOO IX) show Tycho drafting paratexts for the print that the manuscript tradition does not carry.

works.title_en: Additions to the apologetic reply to the Scot Craig
works.gloss: Preface and supplementary documents assembled for a printed edition of the reply to John Craig, recounting the course of the controversy over the celestial location of the comet of 1577 and its sequel — Craig's counter-tract Capnurania and the letters exchanged with the chancellor of Scotland (Joh. date.basis: the edition's year 1589 (grouped with the Apologia); internal references show composition continuing into the early 1590s.
date.correction: The edition's 1589 is the year of the Apologia the dossier was to accompany; the connective matter was assembled for a printed edition projected in the 1590s and never made.
date.note: Dreyer prints the piece without a year (the half-title, TBOO IX p. 151, carries none, unlike the Apologia's '(1589)' at TBOO IV p. 415). The 1589 of the edition is the date of the Apologia itself; the Additamenta cannot all be that early. The second section refers to Craig's 'Capnuraniae restinctio' as already received 'tertio demum anno' after the Apology was sent (sent 25 Oct. 1589; the Capnurania came with Craig's letter of 27 March 1592, TBOO IV pp. 521–522), and to Tycho's letter of August 'the same year' to the Chancellor of Scotland (19 Aug. 1592, TBOO VII pp. 338–341) and to Craig's mockery of that letter. So the piece post-dates 1592 in its present state; it was drafted while the enlarged Craig dossier was being made ready for the press, a project still alive on 31 Dec. 1598 (letter to Longomontanus) and in early 1601 (Kepler set to write the refutation), and it ends with Tycho's death, 24 Oct. 1601. The opening Praefatio alone could in principle go back to the 1591 Uraniborg printing of the Apologia.

works.summary: Not a work but a small dossier of connective and editorial matter that Tycho drafted for a projected enlarged edition of his second cometary volume (De mundi aetherei recentioribus phaenomenis, 1588 = Progymnasmata tom. II), in which his Apologetic Reply to John Craig, Craig's three letters, and Craig's counter-attack 'Capnuraniae restinctio' were to be printed together. It contains (i) a 'Praefatio in Apologiam sequentem' narrating how Tycho had the cometary volume printed on his own press, sent copies to mathematicians for their censure and some to the Frankfurt fair, and had one carried to a mathematician in Scotland (an opportunity offered by the sailing route and the then-pending royal marriage-alliance between the two kingdoms), only for Craig alone to oppose him; (ii) a passage, prefaced by a German instruction to the compositor ('So bald wan die Capnurania auss ist, sollen dissen nachfolgende wordt mitt kleine antiquis gesetz werden' — as soon as the Capnurania ends, set the following words in small roman), dismissing the Capnurania as arrogant and futile, recalling that it reached him amid unwelcome legal business and was read aloud to him by a student on the boat to the Diet at Copenhagen, and declaring that he would not answer it; and (iii) a short linking note announcing the letter of the Scottish Chancellor to Tycho and Tycho's reply. The set is the visible seam of a book that was never finished.
works.occasion: The dispute with John Craig. Tycho sent Craig a copy of De mundi (inscribed at Uraniborg 2 Nov. 1588, now Edinburgh University Library); Craig answered in 1589 with three letters defending the Aristotelian sublunary comet against Tycho's parallax argument; Tycho wrote the Apologetica responsio and sent it to him on 25 Oct. 1589. Having decided to make the whole exchange public by appending it to his second book — and, after Craig's mocking 'Capnuraniae restinctio' arrived in March 1592, to append that too — Tycho wrote these supplementary pieces as the front matter, the transitional note and the closing link of the enlarged volume. The German note to the typesetter shows they were written as printer's copy; the surviving manuscripts of Craig's letters and of the Capnurania carry gathering-numbers showing they had actually been handed to a compositor (TBOO IV p. 522). The book never appeared: Longomontanus was ordered to write the refutation and had not done so by 31 Dec. 1598; Kepler began one about the start of 1601 and abandoned it when Tycho died.
works.addressee_note: No dedicatee. The Praefatio addresses the reader of the projected volume ('optime et benevole Lector'); the adversary throughout is John Craig (d. 1620), the Edinburgh physician-mathematician, Wittich's sometime associate, later physician to James VI. The third section introduces the Chancellor of Scotland, 'Ioannes Metellanus' — John Maitland of Thirlestane — who had visited Tycho at Uraniborg in the retinue of James VI and to whom Tycho wrote on 19 Aug. 1592 (TBOO VII pp. 338–341); the Chancellor's letter to Tycho of 16 May 1592 (TBOO VII pp. 336–337) was to follow at this point in the book.
works.transmission: The words survive in a single manuscript witness: Vienna, Oesterreichische Nationalbibliothek, cod. Vindobonensis lat. 9737f (the volume that also preserves part of Tycho's dealings with and about Craig, and the Craig correspondence Dreyer printed in TBOO VII). Dreyer's source-note at TBOO IX p. 152 reads 'edimus e codice Vindobonensi lat. 9737 f', and his Annotationes (TBOO IX p. 320) say 'Addimus nunc pauca eodem pertinentia e codice Vindobonensi lat. 9737 f' — i.e. first publication. The related texts are edited elsewhere in the same edition: the Apologia from Copenhagen KB Ny kgl. Saml. 93b fol., collated with the Berlin copy (TBOO IV pp. 415–476), the Capnuraniae restinctio fragment from cod. Vindob. lat. 10686 (TBOO IV pp. 477–488), and the Craig and Maitland letters in TBOO VII.
works.channel_basis: first printed in TBOO IX (this catalogue)

printed.note: Nielsen has no entry for these Additamenta, and no authority states that they were ever set in type. What Nielsen's material does record is (a) the Apologia itself, printed at Uraniborg in 1591 — not in his numbered series, contested by Friis and Dreyer on Gassendi's authority, but attested by Rasmus (Erasmus) Bartholin, De cometis (Copenhagen 1665) p. 49, who owned a printed copy; no copy survives; and (b) a contested lost enlarged Apologia said to be '[Wandesburgi] 1598' (Houzeau & Lancaster 1887), for which the evidence is Tycho's letter to Scultetus of 7 Jan. 1600 about 'apologetica' printed in Hamburg — a claim Norlind 1970 corrects Nielsen on. If such an enlarged reissue existed, matter of this kind could conceivably have been set for it; but no copy is known, and nothing in Dreyer connects these particular pages to any press. Treat as unprinted in Tycho's lifetime and first published by Dreyer and Raeder in TBOO IX (Copenhagen 1927), pp. 151–157.

open_questions: Exact date. Dreyer prints the piece undated; DSL/tekstnet dates it 1589 (the Apologia's year). The internal evidence (the Capnurania received in the third year after Oct. 1589; the August 1592 letter to the Scottish Chancellor; Craig's mockery of that letter) puts the second and third sections in or after late 1592, but nothing fixes them more closely within 1592–1601.

Which press was the German compositor's note written for? A German-speaking typesetter served Tycho both on Hven and later; if the instruction belongs to the Wandsbek/Hamburg phase (Philip de Ohr, 1597-98) it would connect these pages to the contested lost enlarged Apologia of 1598. Undetermined — Dreyer says nothing about it.

Whether any of this matter was ever set in type. The manuscripts of Craig's letters and of the Capnurania carry compositor's gathering-numbers (TBOO IV p. 522); it is not stated whether cod. Vindob. lat. 9737f shows the same, and no printed copy of any enlarged Apologia survives.
Whether the opening Praefatio was drafted for the 1591 Uraniborg printing of the Apologia rather than for the later enlarged compilation; it does not itself mention the Capnurania.

Whether Resenius (Inscriptiones Haffnienses, 1668, p. 391) was describing a real printed compilation — Apologia + Craig's letter + Capnuraniae restinctio appended to the second book of the Progymnasmata — or conflating Tycho's plan with the book. Dreyer reports him without endorsement.

B. | Anno 1592, die 15 Febr. in itinere a Ringstadio domum' (TBOO IX, p. 192; Danske Magazin II, 1746, p. 279, where the editors print from Tycho's own autograph draft). Dreyer repeats the date in his 1890 biography ('In February 1592 Tycho had to attend the provincial court at Ringsted', p. 220). The year 1588 given by the edition's index, which files the piece under 1588, immediately after the four epigrams on the death of Frederik II (printed on the same TBOO page, from the same Langebek excerpt-volume) — is therefore wrong or at best unexplained; see open_questions. Composed 15 February 1592, on the ride home from Ringsted.

works.summary: A short, angry epigram: four elegiac couplets, eight lines, untitled in the sources and cited by its incipit. It tells a judge what a judge is for — 'Iudicis est aequi verum rectumque tueri, / Non obstare bonis nilque iuvare malos' (it is the part of a fair judge to uphold what is true and right, not to obstruct the good and give no help against the wicked) — then accuses him of doing the opposite: 'Tu tamen impulsum (testis Deus) aequa movere / Negligis et nequam fersque fovesque malum' (you, God is my witness, neglect to move the just cause when pressed, and you bear with and foster the worthless wrongdoer). It closes on a threat and a barb: the avenger of right and wrong will soon exact the penalty for an insolent cause, so 'if you are wise, look to your own safety, Lago; and if you will not spare me, spare yourself' ('Si sapis ergo, tuae bene consule, Lago, saluti, / Et mihi si non vis parcere, parce tibi'). It is signed 'T. B.' and subscribed with the date and place of composition — on the road home from Ringsted, 15 February 1592.
works.occasion: A lawsuit lost. Tycho had been at the Sjællandsfar landsting (the provincial court of Zealand, which sat at Ringsted), the judgment went against him, and he wrote the epigram on the ride home the same day — the subscription 'in itinere a Ringstadio domum' says as much, and the 1746 Danske Magazin biographer draws exactly that inference: Tycho 'evidently' had a suit before the Sjællandsfar landsting early in 1592 in which the verdict must have gone against him, 'for he gives all too plain expression to his dissatisfaction with the landsdommer Lage Bek, and holds that the greatest injustice has been done him by him' (DM II, p. 279). Dreyer, editing the Carmina in 1927, identifies the litigation as Tycho's long, ugly suit with his tenant Rasmus Pedersen (Erasmus Petri) of Gundsømagle, a peasant on Tycho's Roskilde prebend whom he had put in irons, carried to Hven and held six weeks in prison, and whose case Tycho had lost before four commissioners (April 1591) and again on appeal before the king's Retterting (10 July 1591) — cross-referring to the documents at TBOO XIV pp. 57 ff. and 63 ff. Parts of that matter had been remitted to the herredsting and the landsting, which is why it came before the landsdommer at all. Both eighteenth- and twentieth-century editors hedge on WHICH of the outstanding cases was tried that day (see open_questions), but the general occasion — a judgment against Tycho at Ringsted on 15 February 1592, in the litigation with Rasmus Pedersen — is as well grounded as anything in this register.
works.addressee_note: Lave (Lauge, Lage) Beck, landsdommer of Zealand — addressed only by the vocative 'Lago' in line 7, and identified by both editorial traditions: 'Landsdommeren Lage Bek' (Danske Magazin II, 1746, p. 279) and 'scriptum est ad Lagonem (Lauge) Beck judicem' (Dreyer, TBOO IX, p. 323). He is the Lauge Beck who appears constantly in the chancery registers as lensmand of Roskildegaard and, in the royal letters of 17 November and 1 December 1592, as 'landtzdommer wdj Sieland', ordered by Christian IV's regency government to take the whole Tycho–Rasmus Pedersen quarrel before him and judge it without further delay (TBOO XIV, nos. 96 and 98). Per Toftgaard 2023 he is Lave Beck til Førslev (1530–1607), who held Ringsted abbey as a fief from 1592 and lived there 1592–1605. He is not a member of Tycho's familia and has no entry in Christianson's Biographical Directory.
works.transmission: Manuscript, in two eighteenth-century Copenhagen antiquarian channels, converging on the Royal Library. (1) Tycho's OWN DRAFT. The Danske Magazin editors state that they print from 'Tyge Brahes egenhændige Udkast' — Tycho's autograph draft — 'iblandt de rare Papirer, som Hr. Etats Raad Gram har haft den Godhed i denne Materie at meddele os', i.e. among the rare papers communicated to them by Hans Gram (1685–1748), royal historiographer and librarian (DM II, 1746, p. 279). That is the source of the first printing. (2) LANGEBEK'S EXCERPTS. Dreyer's copy-text in TBOO IX (1927), p. 192, is a different witness: his lemma reads '[Ex excerptis Langebekianis Hauniensibus nr. 179]' — the excerpt-volumes of Jacob Langebek (1710–75) in the Royal Library, Copenhagen. The same excerpt-volume supplied the four chronogram epigrams on Frederik II's death printed immediately above it on the same page; the neighbouring volume nr. 178 supplied the Vedel epigram at TBOO IX, p. 174, of which Dreyer expressly says it is there 'ipsius Tychonis manu scriptum' (TBOO IX, p. 322). He says nothing of the kind for nr. 179, and whether Gram's autograph draft is the very leaf Langebek's collection preserved is not stated by any authority consulted (open question). Dreyer's editorial note identifying the addressee and the lawsuit is at TBOO IX, p. 323. The words therefore survive because two eighteenth-century Danish antiquaries thought a nobleman's private insult to a judge worth copying, not because Tycho ever published it.

printed.note: not printed in Tycho's lifetime, and NOT first printed in TBOO — both would be easy errors here. Nielsen (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600; Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen) has no entry for it, and can have none: it is a private lampoon on a sitting judge, written in the saddle, and there is no trace of a sixteenth-century printing at Uraniborg or anywhere else. Its first appearance in print is posthumous, 154 years after composition: Danske Magazin, Bind II (Copenhagen, 1746), 21. Hefte, p. 279, inside the anonymous 'Efterretninger om Tyge Brahes Levnet', where it is printed in full from Tycho's autograph draft. A German version of that life carried it further: Dreyer cites 'Weistritz, ii. p. 226' alongside the Danske Magazin page (Tycho Brahe, 1890, p. 220 n. 1) — i.e. Philander von der Weistritz's translation of the Danish Magazine life. Dreyer reprinted the text in TBOO IX (1927), p. 192, from a different witness; that is the standard citation today, but it is not the first printing. The publisher/printer of the 1746 Danske Magazin volume has not been verified here and is left blank.

open_questions: WHICH lawsuit was decided at Ringsted on 15 February 1592? No authority states it outright. The Danske Magazin biographer (1746) says only 'perhaps one of the cases mentioned in the Herredags-Dom printed above' (i.e. the Retterting judgment of 10 July 1591 in the Rasmus Pedersen matter, which had remitted some points to the herredsting and some to the landsting); Dreyer 1890, p. 220, says the case was 'probably one of those referred to the provincial court by the Commissioners'; Dreyer 1927 (TBOO IX, p. 323) states it as the Rasmus Pedersen suit but hedges with 'videtur'. Norlind adds that neither the beginning nor the end of that process is fully clear in the documents. No landsting record has been consulted here. The occasion is therefore secure in kind (a judgment against Tycho, before Lave Beck, at Ringsted) but not in the precise cause of action.

The year 1588. The edition's index files this epigram under 1588, while the poem's own subscription — in both print traditions, one of them taken from Tycho's autograph draft — reads 'Anno 1592, die 15 Febr.'. The likeliest explanation is a grouping artefact: in TBOO IX the epigram sits immediately below the four chronogram epigrams on Frederik II's death (1588), from the same Langebek excerpt-volume, on the same page (p. 192). Whether the edition argues for 1588 or merely files the piece there is not stated in its metadata. If the edition does argue for 1588, that is a live disagreement with Dreyer and with the eighteenth-century editors; if it is a slip, the year is 1592.

Does Tycho's autograph draft survive, and is it the witness Dreyer used? Danske Magazin (1746) printed from 'Tyge Brahes egenhændige Udkast' among Hans Gram's papers; Dreyer (1927) printed from 'excerpta Langebekiana nr. 179' in the Royal Library. Both collections ended in the Royal Library, and for the neighbouring volume nr. 178 Dreyer explicitly notes a Tycho autograph — but he does not say that of nr. 179, and no source consulted here identifies the two witnesses with each other. The Langebek excerpt-volume 179 should be inspected.

'Lago' is the only name in the poem. The identification with Lave/Lauge Beck rests entirely on the eighteenth-century editors and on Dreyer, not on the text; it is strongly corroborated by Beck's office (landsdommer of Zealand), by the Ringsted venue, and by the chancery letters of Nov–Dec 1592, but the epigram itself names no surname.

Whether the epigram was ever actually sent or shown to Beck, or remained a private discharge of temper, is unknown. It is subscribed like a letter ('T. B.') but no address, no recipient copy, and no reaction from Beck is recorded in any source consulted.

works.summary: A long poem in elegiac couplets addressed to Denmark personified, opening 'Dania, quid merui, quo te, mea Patria, laesi, / Usque adeo ut rebus sis minus aequa meis?' Tycho asks what he did to deserve his fatherland's ingratitude, rehearses what he built and gave (Uraniborg; the restoration of astronomy, propping up a heaven whose 'orbits' Ptolemy, Alfonso and Copernicus had got wrong; free medicine dispensed to the sick, for which Norway and Sweden will speak if Denmark will not), scorns the ignorant emissary sent to inspect the instruments on Hven, and turns his expulsion into freedom: he is no exile, for the whole world is now his fatherland ('Nunc mihi pro Patria maximus orbis adest'). He expressly exonerates King Christian IV ('Inscius hic culpa, Rex generose, vacas') and lays the blame on a few envious enemies, and he closes by saluting his host Henrik Rantzau at Wandsbek. Resen's 1668 heading calls it an 'elegia hecatonsticha' — an elegy of a hundred lines.
works.occasion: His self-imposed exile. Tycho left Hven with his household on 29 April 1597, moved to Copenhagen, then to Rostock, and in October 1597 to Henrik Rantzau's castle of Wandsbek. On 20 October, the day he resumed at Wandsbek the observations broken off at Hven at the spring equinox, he entered into his observation log first a prose account of his departure ('De occasione interruptarum observationum & discessus mei', TBOO XIII, pp. 101–102) and then, immediately after it, this elegy. It is his apologia and indictment: the poem alludes to the inspection of Hven by the professors Thomas Fincke and Iver Stub (Dreyer 1890, p. 240), exonerates the young king, and thanks Rantzau. Copies went out at once to his correspondents; Rantzau kept one so prominently that Christian IV came upon it and read it through in silence (Dreyer 1890, pp. 254–55; Thoren 1990, p. 385).
works.addressee_note: Denmark itself ('Dania'), his fatherland, apostrophised throughout. Two living persons are addressed within the poem: King Christian IV (1577–1648), 'magnanimi Friderici Heroica proles', explicitly cleared of blame; and, in the closing salute, Henrik Rantzau (1526–1598), the Holstein royal governor, humanist and 'multos per annos fautor... Tychonis' (Dreyer, TBOO IX, p. 323), who housed Tycho at Wandsbek.
works.transmission: Two recensions, both edited by Dreyer. (1) The log recension: Tycho wrote the elegy into his own observation journal for 1596-97 — Dreyer's Codex G, 'Ant. Coll. Reg. 316' = Copenhagen, Kongelige Bibliotek, GKS 2 fol. 316 — immediately after the prose 'De occasione interruptarum obseruationum & discessus mej' (Dreyer, TBOO X, Prolegomena, p. XVIII); the passage is in Tycho's own hand, with the colophon of 20 October 1597. Dreyer printed it there at TBOO XIII (1926), pp. 102–104. (2) The collected recension: Tycho later gathered his own poems, and the fair copy in Vienna, Cod. Vindobonensis lat. 10686, carries a lightly revised text; Dreyer printed that among the Carmina at TBOO IX (1927), pp. 208–211, noting 'quamquam inter observationes inseruit Tycho, et nos inter has edidimus (tom. XIII p. 102 sqq.), tamen hic quoque non deesse voluimus... hic correctiones paucas intulimus, quae Tychoni carmina sua colligenti magis placuerant, ut e Vindobonensi codice patet' (TBOO IX, p. 327). Manuscript copies were circulated: Rantzau's, stitched into his printed Calendarium Ranzovianum (Hamburg 1590), was the copy King Christian IV found and read; the copy Tycho sent to Joseph Scaliger in 1598 (23 pp. folio), carrying Tycho's own note on that episode, is in the University Library at Leiden (Dreyer 1890, p. 255 and n. 3; the same story is in Danske Magazin II, p. 340 sq., and was told again to Herwart von Hohenburg). So the words survive first in Tycho's autograph observation journal, and TBOO is the critical, not the first, printing.

printed.nielsen: none — no printing of the elegy is recorded among Tycho's printed works
printed.note: not printed in Tycho's lifetime. Nielsen (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600; Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen, 1921) records no printing of it, and Tycho's press had left Hven with him in April 1597; Dreyer states plainly that 'copies of the poem were sent to various correspondents' in manuscript (1890, p. 255), and Christian IV had in any case forbidden Tycho to print his letter to the king (Thoren 1990, p. 385). The poem first reached print posthumously. Dreyer (1890, p. 254 n. 2) lists the early printed texts: Historia Coelestis (ed. 'Lucius Barrettus' [Albert Curtz], Augsburg 1666), p. 802; Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Copenhagen 1668), p. 347 — verified on the page image, headed 'Wandesburgi An: 1597 die Octobris Elegiam Hecatonsticham condidit Tycho Brahaeus quae haec est'; Casseburg, Tychonis Brahe relatio de statu suo (Jena 1730); and 'less correctly given by Gassendi, p. 143' (Tychonis Brahei... Vita, 1st ed. Paris 1654; 2nd ed. The Hague 1655) — which, if Dreyer's page reference is right, is the earliest printing by date, though it was not inspected here. Extracts also in Danske Magazin II (Copenhagen 1746), p. 340 sqq.

open_questions: The true first printing has not been verified page-in-hand. By date, Gassendi's Vita (Paris 1654; 2nd ed. The Hague 1655), p. 143 in Dreyer's citation, precedes Historia Coelestis (1666) and Resen (1668); Dreyer calls Gassendi's text the least correct. Gassendi's page was not inspected, so 'first printed by Gassendi' is asserted only on Dreyer's authority, not on autopsy.

Whether the copy Rantzau kept in his printed Calendarium Ranzovianum (Hamburg 1590) — the one Christian IV read — was manuscript or a print is not stated by Dreyer. No printed copy of the elegy from Tycho's lifetime is known, and the Scaliger copy is manuscript, so the presumption is manuscript.
The exact verse count of each recension was not established here; Resen's 1668 heading calls it a 'hecatonsticha' (hundred-line) elegy, and the two TBOO texts differ slightly in wording.

works.title: Ad Daniam elegia (fra observationsprotokollen)
works.title_full: Ad Daniam elegia (fra observationsprotokollen)
works.title_en: Elegy to Denmark (from the observation protocol)
works.gloss: Prose account from the observation protocol of why Tycho broke off his observations and left Denmark in 1597, followed by his farewell elegy to Denmark, entered at Wandsbek and dated 20 October 1597.

date.basis: Tycho's own colophon in the text: 20 October 1597 at Wandsbek; all internal events (departure from Hven 29 April, Rostock, Rantzau's Wandsbek) are 1597; corroborated by the survey of the autograph passages in GKS 316 (Observationes).
date.correction: Tycho's own colophon in the observation log: 20 October 1597, Wandsbek. The edition's 1573 is a metadata error on the source site.
date.note: Subscribed in the autograph: 'T. B. feci / Anno Domini 1597 20 die Octobris cum Wandesburgi Observationes Astronomicas antea circa Aequinoctium vernum Uraniburgi inuite omissas continuare coepi' (TBOO XIII, p. 104). Dreyer 1890, p. 253, dates the entry to 20 October 1597 at Wandsbek. The year 1573 carried by the edition's metadata is contradicted by the autograph colophon and by the poem's whole subject-matter (the 1597 departure from Denmark, the six children in exile, Rantzau's hospitality at Wandsbek); the year is 1597.

works.summary: An elegy of some fifty-one elegiac couplets (c. 102 lines), opening 'Dania quid merui, quo te mea Patria laesi', in which Tycho arraigns his native country for repaying his services with ingratitude. It recites what he did for Denmark's fame, mocks the ignorant emissary sent to inspect Hven who sneered at instruments he could not name, sets his own labours beside those of Hercules and against the errors of Ptolemy, the Alfonsine tables and Copernicus, recalls the medicines he gave the sick without charge, and turns from complaint to release: he is no exile, for the whole world is now his country. It exculpates King Christian IV by name ('magnanimi Friderici Heroica proles') and closes with a salute to Heinrich Rantzau, who first gave Urania lodging, at his castle of Wandsbek near Hamburg. In the observation journal it stands immediately after Tycho's prose account of why the observations stopped, 'De occasione interruptarum observationum et discessus mei' (TBOO XIII, pp. 101–102).
works.occasion: The resumption of observing in exile. Tycho had left Hven on 29 April 1597 and Denmark before midsummer; after a quarter-year at Rostock he accepted Heinrich Rantzau's invitation and moved to Wandsbek in mid-October 1597. On 20 October, at the point in the observation journal where the Wandsbek observations begin, he wrote in first the prose statement of the causes of the interruption and of his departure, and then this elegy as its verse counterpart (TBOO XIII, pp. 101–104; Dreyer 1890, pp. 253–254). The occasion is thus documented, not inferred: the poem is the emotional settlement of accounts entered into the working record at the moment observing began again.
works.addressee_note: Denmark itself, apostrophised throughout ('Dania quid merui...'); there is no dedicatee in the formal sense. Within the poem King Christian IV is expressly exculpated, and the closing paragraph salutes the host, Heinrich Rantzau (1526–1598), royal Statthalter of the royal portions of Schleswig-Holstein, builder of Wandsbek, and Tycho's protector there from October 1597 to autumn 1598. Manuscript copies were sent to correspondents: Tycho sent one to Joseph Scaliger (Dreyer 1890, p. 255 n. 3, reporting it then in the University Library at Leiden), and he related the same story to Herwart von Hohenburg.
works.transmission: Autograph. Tycho entered the elegy in his own hand into the observation journal now Copenhagen, Kongelige Bibliotek, GKS 316 fol. — Dreyer's siglum G, 'Codex Hauniensis Ant. Coll. Reg. 316' (TBOO IX, Varia scripturae, p. 316, s.v. 'Ad elegiam in Daniam'), the volume of the 1596-97 observations — immediately after the prose 'De occasione interruptarum observationum et discessus mei' and immediately before the Wandsbek observations, subscribed 20 October 1597. Dreyer printed this text in situ among the 1597 observations at TBOO XIII (1926), pp. 102–104. A second recension survives in Vienna, cod. Vindob. lat. 10686 (fasc. 49) — Dreyer's siglum V — representing the few corrections Tycho preferred later, when he was collecting his poems, and carrying the appended prose anecdote of Christian IV reading the poem at Haderslev; Dreyer printed that recension among the Carmina at TBOO IX (1927), pp. 208–211, stating expressly that the poem was one Tycho 'inserted among the observations, and we have edited it among them (tom. XIII p. 102 sqq.)', giving in vol. XIII the text as Tycho first had it written and in vol. IX the poet's later corrections (TBOO IX, Annotationes editorum, p. 327). The two recensions differ in a handful of readings (e.g. XIII 'Nostra licet iamnunc gratia muta silet' against IX 'Gratia sit nostro tempore muta licet'; XIII 'ut fertur' against IX 'ut referunt'). Additional witnesses: the copy Tycho sent Scaliger (Leiden), and the copy Rantzau bound into his Calendarium Ranzovianum. TBOO is thus not the first printing (see the printed block).
works.channel_basis: the observation log GKS 316; TBOO XIII

printed.note: not printed in Tycho's lifetime, and not printed by Tycho at all: it has no entry in Nielsen's bibliography of the printed Tycho corpus (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600 / Bogtrykkeri paa Hveen), which records nothing of the kind for the Wandsbek year beyond the Mechanica and its companions. The poem circulated in manuscript (Rantzau had a copy stitched into his Calendarium Ranzovianum, where King Christian IV came upon it at Haderslev). The printings are all posthumous, the earliest cited by Dreyer being Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei... Vita (Paris, 1654), p. 143, 'less correctly' given; the observation-journal text then reached print in the Historia Coelestis, p. 802 (the folio edition of Tycho's observations, i.e. the very manuscript this recension stands in), and again in P. J. Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses (Copenhagen, 1668), p. 347, and in Casseburg, Tychonis Brahe relatio de statu suo (Jena, 1730). See Dreyer 1890, p. 254 nn. 1-2.

B. feci... 1597' colophon), while the page at brahe-t_ad-daniam-elegia-2 carries the Vienna recension (anchored [TBOO IX.208-211], with [V 1r]-[V 2r] leaf sigla and the Christian IV prose note). This record keeps the key (-2) and the title ('fra observationsprotokollen'), i.e. it documents the observation-journal recension.
The edition's year 1573 for both records is wrong (autograph colophon: 20 October 1597); its publication-year field reads 1573 for several unrelated Tycho texts as well.

Which recension Gassendi printed in the Vita (1654), p. 143, and whether he gave the whole poem, has not been verified against Gassendi himself (his page was not inspected); Dreyer says only that it is 'less correctly given'.

Beyond the Scaliger copy (Leiden) and the copy stitched into Rantzau's Calendarium Ranzovianum, the 'copies sent to various correspondents' (Dreyer 1890, p. 255) have not been enumerated; a census of surviving manuscript copies of the elegy remains to be done.

works.title: Ad Martinum Braschium
works.title_full: Ad Martinum Braschium
works.gloss: Epigram for the Rostock poet Martin Brasch, written in Tycho's own hand on a wrapper of gold coins sent in thanks for a poem Brasch had addressed to him, and alluding to the philosopher's stone Brasch had promised. Behind it lies a larger correspondence in which Tycho acted as editor of his own praise: he rejected a philosophical poem Brasch offered as unsuited to the imperial court, steered him instead to a didactic poem on the famous astronomers, and supplied the bibliography, directions for its composition, and the first seven verses in his own draft.

date.basis: Undated in the text; Tycho's documented contact with Martin Brasch runs from his Rostock stay of 1597 to April 1601 (Norlind 1970, pp. 168, 199, 339; TBOO VIII letters), and TBOO IX prints the epigram at IX 208 immediately before the October 1597 farewell elegy in its chronological sequence.
date.correction: The range 1597–1601 spans Tycho's documented contact with Brasch; the epigram belongs to the Rostock stay of 1597 (Dreyer prints it before the October 1597 elegy). The edition's 1573 is a metadata error.
date.note: The epigram itself is undated in the manuscript. It is dated by its occasion, which Dreyer states: Brasch wrote the poem it answers when Tycho, having left his native country, came to Rostock in the year 1597 ('cum a. 1597 Rostochium Tycho venisset patria relicta, carmen scripserat »Ad Tychonem Brahe in Germaniam transeuntem«, quod inter chartas Tychonis reperitur; post hoc reperitur epigramma, quod attulimus', TBOO IX, p. 327). Tycho was at Rostock from about midsummer to mid-October 1597, then at Wandsbek; the reply could have been sent from either place, so 1597 (or very early 1598) is the honest bracket. Its position in Dreyer's Carmina, immediately before the Ad Daniam elegia of 20 October 1597 (IX 208-211), agrees with a 1597 date. The edition's year 1573 is impossible: Martin Brasch was born in 1565 (TBOO VIII, Index virorum doctorum, p. 453); it is the same metadata artefact as on the two Ad Daniam elegia records. Nor is the piece a letter: it is a four-line epigram, printed by Dreyer among the Carmina, not among the Epistolae.

works.summary: A four-line Latin epigram in two elegiac couplets (incipit 'Haec Aganippeae pro vena munera venae / Auriferae, Braschi, consule missa boni'), which Tycho wrote in his own hand on the slip of paper in which he wrapped a few gold coins as a thank-offering to the Rostock poet Martin Brasch. The prose rubric that carries it in the manuscript sets out the whole transaction: the poet had sent his poem to Tycho by a student known to him; Tycho ordered a reply to be carried back by the same man, and 'subscribed the following epigram in my own hand' on the little sheet, 'in which I was wrapping some gold coins by way of gratitude', enclosed with the letter. The verses turn on a pun on vena: the gold-bearing vein (the coins) repays the Aganippean vein (Brasch's poetic inspiration, Aganippe being the Muses' spring). They close on an alchemical joke — when that potent Stone of the Sages which you promise ('lapis ille Sophorum, quem spondes') has yielded its many talents of gold, you shall have more.
works.occasion: Recoverable, and stated by Dreyer. It is a payment-and-thanks piece. Brasch had written a laudatory poem, 'Ad Tychonem Brahe in Germaniam transeuntem' ('To Tycho Brahe crossing over into Germany'), on Tycho's arrival at Rostock in 1597 after he had left Denmark; that poem survives among Tycho's papers, and the epigram stands immediately after it in the same manuscript (TBOO IX, p. 327). Tycho's answer was a fee: gold coins wrapped in a paper, with these four lines written on the wrapper in his own hand and sent back by the student who had brought the poem. What exactly Brasch had 'promised' (quem spondes) — whether his poem predicted that Tycho's chymistry would achieve the philosophers' stone, or whether Brasch had pledged something of his own — is not explained by Dreyer and is not recoverable from the four lines alone.
works.addressee_note: Martin Brasch (Martinus Braschius), born 1565, professor of logic at Rostock, died 1601; 'auctor est carminum atque orationum multarum' (TBOO VIII, Index virorum doctorum, p. 453). Tycho calls him 'Poeta Rostochiensis' and, with Taubmann, one of the 'Poetae laureati' who supplied him with verse. He is not a member of the Hven familia and does not appear in Christianson's Biographical Directory; he belongs to the exile years. From 1598 he sent Tycho a series of laudatory poems — heroic, lyric and elegiac — which Tycho collected, criticised and corrected with a view to printing them with his own works (Tycho to Oliger Rosenkrantz, 28 June 1598 and 9 Sept. 1598, TBOO VIII 75 and 110; to Paulus Melissus, 7/17 Feb. 1600, VIII 249). Seven letters between them survive: Tycho to Brasch 19/29 March 1600, 5/15 Sept. 1600, 6/16 Nov. 1600, 4/14 April 1601 (TBOO VIII 290-291, 357-360, 391, 410-413); Brasch to Tycho 8/18 Aug. 1600, 20/30 Sept. 1600, 8/18 March 1601 (VIII 337-339, 379-380, 402).
works.transmission: Manuscript, in the Vienna Tycho papers. Dreyer's source lemma is '[E codice Vindobonensi lat. 10686...]' (the printed siglum carries a superscript sub-number), and his marginal folio mark in the text is 9v — i.e. Oesterreichische Nationalbibliothek, Cod. Vind. lat. 10686, fol. 9r-v. That codex is one of the fair copies made for the printers of the never-finished Epistolarum astronomicarum liber secundus and is the manuscript from which Dreyer and Raeder drew most of the letters in TBOO VII (TBOO VII 393-394). The epigram stands there immediately after Brasch's own poem 'Ad Tychonem Brahe in Germaniam transeuntem', which Dreyer saw among the same papers but did not print (it is not Tycho's). First published by J. L. E. Dreyer and J. Raeder, Tychonis Brahe Dani Opera Omnia IX (Hauniae, 1927), Carmina, p. 208, with the editors' note at p. 327; indexed in TBOO XV, s.v. 'Brasch, Martinus, poeta': 'epigramma Tychonis ad eum IX 208'.
works.channel_basis: first printed in TBOO IX (this catalogue)

printed.note: Not printed in Tycho's lifetime. It was a private note written on the wrapper of a coin-gift, and Lauritz Nielsen's enumerative bibliography of Tycho's whole printed output (Dansk Bibliografi 1551–1600, the 12 publications and 4 lost prints) contains no such item. Tycho did nevertheless mean it for print: the text was copied into one of the fair-copy manuscripts written out 'nitide in typographorum usum' for the projected Epistolarum astronomicarum liber secundus, in which, as he announced in the 1596 preface to Book I, 'Carmina nonnulla... a nobis interdum animi caussa conscripta' were to be interwoven with the letters (TBOO VI 22; TBOO VII 393-394). That volume was broken off after half an alphabet when Tycho left Hven in 1597, was abandoned by his heirs, and no printed quire of it is known to survive — so the epigram never reached print in his lifetime. Dreyer prints it from the Vienna manuscript and, unlike his practice elsewhere in the Carmina (where he names Resen 1668 for the Urania Titani, Gassendi for the Mechanica epigram, Vingaard's 1572 broadsheet for the Fratri gemello), records no earlier printing. On present evidence the first printing is TBOO IX (Copenhagen 1927), p. 208; that it was never printed earlier is an argument from Dreyer's and Nielsen's silence, not a positive statement by either.

references.locus: the complete chronological corpus (12 publications, §§424–433, §§975–976) and the four known lost prints
references.supports: That no printing of this epigram forms any part of Tycho's printed output — i.e. it was not printed in his lifetime

references.source: Dreyer & Raeder, TBOO VIII
references.locus: p. 75 (Tycho to Oliger Rosenkrantz, 28 June 1598: 'Misit etiam BRASCHIUS Poeta Rostochiensis Heroicum in mei gratiam concinnatum'), p. 110 (9 Sept. 1598: 'Addidi alterum exemplar versuum BRASCHIJ Poetae Rostochiensis, quod rectius est castigatum atque revisum'), pp. 290–291 (Tycho to Brasch, 19/29 March 1600, criticising Brasch's elegy line by line and reserving the right to alter it)
references.supports: The nature of the relationship: Brasch as a supplier of laudatory verse whose poems Tycho collected, corrected and meant to print — the context in which a fee wrapped in an epigram makes sense

open_questions: The exact date and place. Dreyer fixes Brasch's poem to Tycho's arrival at Rostock in 1597 but does not date the epigram itself, which is undated in the codex. Tycho was at Rostock c. midsummer to mid-October 1597 and at Wandsbek from October; the reply could have been written at either. 1597 is probable, not secure.
The unnamed 'Studiosus quendam mihi notum' who carried Brasch's poem to Tycho and the coins back to Brasch is not identified by Dreyer.

What Brasch 'promised' (lapis ille Sophorum, quem spondes). Whether his poem predicted that Tycho would achieve the philosophers' stone, or whether Brasch was himself making an alchemical promise, is not explained anywhere in TBOO; the joke's target is therefore only half legible.

Whether the epigram was printed anywhere before TBOO IX (1927). Dreyer names prior printings for other Carmina but none here, and Nielsen does not record it; neither, however, positively states that TBOO is the first printing. F. R. Friis's 19th-century publications of Tycho material have not been checked for it.

The precise manuscript siglum. Dreyer prints 'E codice Vindobonensi lat. 10686' with a superscript sub-number; the marginal folio mark on the text is 9v. The sub-part and the present-day OeNB foliation have not been verified against the codex.
editorial_notes: Zeeberg 1993 (pp. 47–48): the Brasch correspondence (TBOO VIII, 290-413) shows Tycho rejecting a philosophical poem of Brasch's as unsuitable for the imperial court, commissioning instead a didactic poem on famous astronomers, and supplying bibliography, directives, and the first seven verses in his own draft — Zeeberg's summary: 'Tycho Brahe er astronomien i egen person' (p. 48).

desiderata.text: Written permission from Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab for the republication of the edition's Danish translations, textual notes and commentary. Until it is given, the pages carry the edition's Latin and link to the translations and the notes at the source.

The translator of the Mechanica's Danish instrument chapters (sections 4–27, 32–33), reproduced by the edition in a pre-1948 orthography; the local copy names no one. The Danish Mechanica of Ræder, Strömgren and Strömgren (Nordisk Astronomisk Tidsskrift, 1948–1955) is the likely source and should be confirmed.

Full records — summary, occasion, addressee, printing, transmission, references, open questions, grade — for the 28 texts that carry only their identifying fields. The 29 researched records set the standard.

The Latin of Occasio et argumentum, which the edition prints only in Danish; Dreyer prints it at TBOO IX 324–326 from cod. Vindob. lat. 10686. A transcription from the page images would make the record a Latin–Danish pair.
Dreyer's text of every work here, from the page imagess of the Opera omnia, as a second witness beside the edition's text — the public-domain fallback should the edition's permission be refused.
The edition's key to its witness sigla, which the harvest did not capture; sigla are listed per text as they occur, with a meaning only where the note itself gives one.
The entries of the Epistolae astronomicae that could not be joined to an Epistolarium letter on their date alone (listed in §5); each wants a hand join.
The letters of Jerónimo Muñoz appended to the preface for the second volume have no Epistolarium record; the authorship of the letter dated 6 December is to be settled against TBOO VII 395–403.
The Kronborg inscriptions have no site record in Loca; the bridge waits on one.
Horoscopi has no per-item anchors; the three nativities, the almanac preface and the fragment link to the pillar page only.

Persons named on these pages who have no Familia record: Niels Kaas, Jacob Ulfeldt, Hans Frandsen, Lauge Beck, Rudolphus Caukerchius, Jerónimo Muñoz, James VI, the six poets of the Epistolae astronomicae, Tycho's children.
The verse Dreyer prints inside the other volumes (§10 a) is outside the edition; the pieces inside the letters are read in the Epistolarium, the rest only in the Opera omnia.
The edition transmits the figures of the 1573 almanac, the nativity charts and the Mechanica's woodcuts as placeholders; the woodcuts are seen in Instrumenta, the rest only in the scans.

sources.full: Adam Mosley, Bearing the Heavens: Tycho Brahe and the Astronomical Community of the Late Sixteenth Century (Cambridge, 2007).
sources.contributes: The printed correspondence as an instrument of reputation.

sources.full: Günther Oestmann, 'Tycho Brahe's Attitude towards Astrology and his Relations to Heinrich Rantzau', in Tycho Brahe and Prague: Crossroads of European Science (2002).
sources.contributes: The Rantzau connection behind the 1585 poem and the medicaments.

sources.full: Peder Hansen Resen, Inscriptiones Hafnienses Latinae, Danicae et Germanicae (Copenhagen, 1668).
sources.contributes: The only witness for the Uraniborg inscriptions and the printing epigram.

sources.full: Erik Pontoppidan, Marmora Danica, tom. I (Copenhagen, 1739).
sources.contributes: The first printing of the Kronborg inscriptions.

sources.full: Danske Magazin, vol. II (Copenhagen, 1746), the Tycho Brahe documents in the 19th and 21st parts.
sources.contributes: The first printing of the epigram to Lauge Beck, with his name.

sources.full: Pierre Gassendi, Tychonis Brahei, equitis Dani, astronomorum coryphaei, Vita (Paris, 1654; 2nd ed. The Hague, 1655).
sources.contributes: The first printing of the farewell elegy.

sources.full: Wilhelm Norlind, Tycho Brahe: En levnadsteckning med nya bidrag belysande hans liv och verk (Lund, 1970).
sources.contributes: The Brasch contact and the exile chronology.

sources.full: Peter Zeeberg, Den praktiske muse: Tycho Brahes brug af latindigtningen (Copenhagen, 1993).
sources.contributes: The reading of Tycho's Latin poetry as social practice; the Brasch correspondence; the 1584–85 Uraniborg prints.

sources.full: Peter Zeeberg, Urania Titani: Et digt af Tycho Brahe (Copenhagen, 1994).
sources.contributes: The edition and study of the heroic epistle.

sources.full: Peter Zeeberg, 'Den latinske Tycho', in Poul Grinder-Hansen (ed.), Tycho Brahes Verden (Copenhagen, 2006).
sources.contributes: The date of the Ulfeldt poem and the poet's profile.

sources.full: Peter Zeeberg, 'Forfatterskabsportræt: Tycho Brahe', tekstnet.dk (Det Danske Sprog- og Litteraturselskab).
sources.contributes: The editor's own account of the corpus: about a hundred poems, transmitted piecemeal; the edition's selection.

sources.full: Håkan Håkansson (ed.), Att låta själen flyga mellan himlens tinnar: Tycho Brahe och renässansen (Stockholm, 2006).
sources.contributes: The Ulfeldt poem's date and the Swedish reception.

sources.full: Dieter Lohmeier, Heinrich Rantzau: Humanismus und Renaissance in Schleswig-Holstein (Heide, 2000).
sources.contributes: Rantzau's library and the medical compositions.

sources.full: Emil Gigas, 'Nogle Bøger fra Tycho Brahes Bogbinderi', Bogvennen (Copenhagen, 1900).
sources.contributes: The bindings that carry the inscriptions round Tycho's portrait and arms.

sources.full: Francis Beckett and Charles Christensen, Uraniborg og Stjerneborg (Copenhagen, 1921).
sources.contributes: The buildings the inscriptions belonged to.

sources.full: F. R. Friis, Tyge Brahe: En historisk Fremstilling efter trykte og utrykte Kilder (Copenhagen, 1871).
sources.contributes: The documentary narrative of the Danish years.

sources.full: Rasmus Bartholin, De cometis anni MDCLXIV et MDCLXV (Copenhagen, 1665).
sources.contributes: An early reprint of comet material.

sources.full: Elias Olsen Morsing, Diarium astrologicum et meteorologicum anni 1586 (Uraniborg, 1586).
sources.contributes: The book in which the first comet treatise and the finished preface were printed.

sources.full: Jens Vellev, 'Et industrianlæg og en votivsten på Hven fra renæssancen: Om Tycho Brahes papirmølle', Renæssanceforum 12 (2017).
sources.contributes: The paper mill and its inscription stone.

sources.full: Mogens Brøndsted, 'Et ukendt digt af Tycho Brahe', Fund og Forskning 9 (1962).
sources.contributes: A poem outside the Carmina.

sources.full: Anders Toftgaard, 'Battles of Books: Denmark and Heinrich Rantzau' (2023).
sources.contributes: Rantzau's book of medicine.

sources.full: Kancelliets Brevbøger vedrørende Danmarks indre Forhold, 1588–1592 (Copenhagen).
sources.contributes: The royal letters behind the Beck lawsuit.

sources.full: Thesaurus Librorum Danicorum, vol. 2 (nos. 307–745).
sources.contributes: The Aslakssøn printing of the Oration.
